title: Four cooks, one oven
hook: One cook makes 10 pizzas an hour. What do four cooks make in one small kitchen?

knows: that more workers usually means more output
doesNotKnow: that when something else is fixed (the oven), each extra worker often adds less than the one before
that output can stop rising altogether

misconception: Four workers make four times as much as one.
objective: The learner can explain that with a fixed input, each added worker adds less output than the last, so total output grows more slowly than the number of workers and can stop growing.

claims.text: If the first worker adds 10 pizzas an hour and each added worker adds 2 fewer than the last, 4 workers make 28 an hour (10 + 8 + 6 + 4), not 40.
claims.source: 10 + 8 + 6 + 4 = 28; 4 × 10 = 40. Demo.tsx totalOf(4). | v2 (2026-10-14): question no longer states the decrement; reveal gated on seeing worker 6 add nothing; previous verification void, needs re-check.

claims.text: In this model, with one oven, the kitchen tops out at 30 pizzas an hour at 5 workers; worker 6 and later add nothing (the reveal names the highest such worker the learner set, 6, 7 or 8).
claims.source: adds(k) = max(0, 12 − 2k): 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, 0, 0; running totals 10, 18, 24, 28, 30, 30, 30, 30. | v2 (2026-10-14): question no longer states the decrement; reveal gated on seeing worker 6 add nothing; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Numbers verified (own node: adds 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, 0, 0; totals peak 30 at 5; reveal gated on n > 5). DISPUTED on the parenthetical: Demo look() overwrites seen.zero on every one-oven visit past 5, so the reveal names the latest such worker set, not the highest (set 8 then 6: reveal says 6). The learner sentence stays true (6, 7 and 8 all add nothing); the claim text is wrong. Fix (builder): 'the most recent such worker' in the claim text, or keep the max in code. | v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder): kept the claim text ('highest'); Demo look() now stores seen.zero = max(seen.zero, k), so setting 8 then 6 still names 8. Reopened. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own node: one-oven adds 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, 0, 0, totals peak 30 at 5. v4 look() stores max(seen.zero, k) for one-oven k > 5 (also on 'Back to one oven'), so set 8 then 6 names 8.

claims.text: When one input is fixed, adding more of another input eventually adds less and less output (diminishing returns).
claims.source: Diminishing marginal product: 'the marginal product of an input declines as the quantity of the input increases' (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 13). The oven as the fixed input is the lesson's illustration.

claims.text: The increments (10, 8, 6, 4…) are made-up numbers in a model where the only fixed input is the oven: each new cook shares the same oven with one more person and adds 2 fewer than the one before; nothing else changes.
claims.source: Model choice by the builder (Demo.tsx v3 adds()); brief in company/domains/briefs/economics.md. Not a measured kitchen: disclosed on stage ('Model: made-up numbers') and in the reveal's last line. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Model disclosed on the stage chip 'Model: made-up numbers' and the reveal's muted last line; adds() is 10 - 2(k - 1) floored at 0, the oven is the only fixed input in the model.

claims.text: In the same model, a second oven splits the cooks between two ovens, so the k-th worker adds 10 − 2·(⌈k/2⌉ − 1): for example 7 workers make 52 an hour (10+10+8+8+6+6+4) and 8 make 56, against 30 with one oven; fewer cooks per oven, so each adds more. The reveal quotes a two-oven state only when it beats one oven at the same number of workers (2 or more workers), with the one-oven total beside it.
claims.source: Demo.tsx v3 adds(k, 2) and totalOf(n, 2); hand sums: n=4 → 36, n=7 → 52, n=8 → 56. Illustrates that the shrinking increments come from the fixed input (Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 13: diminishing marginal product with a fixed factory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Formula and sums verified (own node: two-oven adds 10, 10, 8, 8, 6, 6, 4, 4; totals 36 at 4, 52 at 7, 56 at 8). DISPUTED: the reveal quotes the last two-oven state, and the learner can reach 1 worker with two ovens (Remove one down to 1, then Add a second oven), giving '1 workers made 10: fewer cooks per oven, so each added more.' With one worker the second oven adds nothing (10 either way), so the sentence is false there (and '1 workers'). Fix (builder): quote the second-oven sentence only when totalOf(n, 2) > totalOf(n, 1) (n >= 2), or quote the n >= 2 state. | v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder): Demo look() records the two-oven state only when totalOf(k, 2) > totalOf(k, 1) (k >= 2), and the reveal re-checks that before quoting it; the reveal now also prints the one-oven total for the same n (e.g. 2 workers: 20, one oven 18). Reopened. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own node: two-oven totals 10, 20, 28, 36, 42, 48, 52, 56 vs one-oven 10, 18, 24, 28, 30, 30, 30, 30; k-th add 10 - 2(ceil(k/2) - 1). v4 records a two-oven state only if totalOf(k, 2) > totalOf(k, 1), which excludes k = 1, and the reveal re-checks it and prints the one-oven total beside it.

recall.question: A café has one espresso machine. Barista 1 serves 30 drinks an hour, barista 2 adds 20, barista 3 adds 10. What best explains the shrinking additions?
options: Later baristas are worse at the job
They all share the same machine
recall.why: With one input fixed (the machine), each extra worker has less of it to use, so each adds less: diminishing returns.
